transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you. Um, I came in because... I just can't seem to stop my mind once a worry starts. It’s like, once I start worrying about my mother getting up at night—she has this awful habit of wandering the house in the dark, and I bought her these little motion-sensor nightlights online, but she unplugs them because she says they use too much electricity, which makes absolutely no sense for an LED, right? 

But anyway, once I start worrying about her, or about a grant report, or whether I missed something at work... I just can’t seem to shelve it in my mind. And I try! I make lists. Being a librarian, well, a media collections specialist, I'm very good at organizing things. We actually just got this huge donation of 16mm films from the local historical society that I've been trying to archive, and they smell strongly of vinegar, which means they're degrading, so I have to keep them separated from the main collection. 

But yeah, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself, the worry just stays stuck in my head.
Do you ever feel like you have to perform specific rituals or actions to reduce your worry?

Um, rituals? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't have to, like, touch a doorknob a certain number of times or wash my hands over and over or anything. I mean, I do have a very specific way I organize my workspace, but that's just because of my job. Like, my archival pens have to be on the exact left side of my keyboard, always. 

Speaking of which, it is getting so incredibly hard to find good quality acid-free pens these days. The supplier we've used for the last ten years just got bought out by some massive corporate conglomerate, and the ink in the new batches takes just a fraction of a second longer to dry. Which doesn't sound like much to most people, I know, but when you're labeling delicate microfilm sleeves, that fraction of a second is the difference between a perfectly clean label and a massive, permanent smudge. I actually had to throw out an entire box of archival sleeves last Tuesday because of it, and they are not cheap. The budget committee is already breathing down my neck about our department's spending... 

But, um... wait, what were you asking? Oh, right, actions to stop the worry. No, I don't do anything like that. I just sit there and worry.
Do you feel a strong need to repeat certain tasks or mental acts to relieve anxiety or worry?

No, not really. I mean, I don't have to repeat things in my head or do tasks over and over to feel better. I just... I just think about the worries a lot. Like a broken record. Speaking of records, we have this massive collection of vinyl at the library, mostly spoken word and local oral histories from the 1960s, and we're supposed to be digitizing them. But the turntable we have is so finicky, and the needle—the stylus—needs to be replaced, but of course, the model is discontinued. I spent three hours on eBay last night trying to find a replacement part, and I finally found one from a seller in Germany, but the shipping is astronomical. I don't know how I'm going to justify that to the budget committee, especially after the whole pen fiasco. They already think the media department is a money pit. 

But, um... no, I don't do anything repeatedly to make the anxiety go away. I wish I did, honestly. Maybe it would help. I just kind of sit with it and let it run laps in my brain.
Is your worry usually about a specific thing or situation, or does it seem to jump around to a lot of different things?

Well, it definitely jumps around. Over this past year, it’s like it started with just worrying about my mother’s safety, with the nightlights and her wandering, but now it’s spread to... everything. Finances, staff decisions at the library, deadlines, the house, whether I'm actually being a good daughter to her... even really small things just feel like they’re about to completely unravel. 

Like the other day, I was looking at the gutters on my house, and they were a little clogged with leaves—we have this enormous oak tree in the front yard, beautiful in the summer, but a total nightmare in the fall. The leaves get absolutely everywhere. Anyway, I started thinking about the gutters, and then suddenly I was convinced the water was going to back up, ruin the roof, leak into the foundation, and I'd be financially ruined and have to sell the house and move my mother into a facility, which she would absolutely hate. 

And speaking of facilities, did you know how much they charge for assisted living these days? I was looking at brochures just... just in case, you know? And the pricing structures are completely opaque. It's like they don't want you to know what you're actually paying for. It reminded me of when we were trying to negotiate the new database subscriptions at work. The vendors give you these bundled packages that include fifty journals you don't need just to get the three you do, and if you try to unbundle them, they charge you double. It's extortion, honestly. The budget committee was furious, but what are we supposed to do? The students need access to the archives. 

But, um... yes, the worry. It definitely jumps from one thing to another. It never just stays on one topic.
Do you feel like your worrying is interfering with your daily life or work in any significant way?

Well, yes, I... I think it really is. It’s starting to affect my work, which terrifies me, honestly. I've always been the person who catches everything. But lately, I’ve started missing these small but important details at the library. Like, I mislabeled an entire series of photographs from the 1920s last week because I was so distracted worrying about my mother. 

And speaking of photographs, we have this incredible collection of glass plate negatives that were donated by a local family, and they are just stunning. The detail you can get on glass plates is something you just don't see with digital photography. But they are so fragile, you have to handle them with these special lint-free gloves, and the humidity in the storage room has to be exactly 40%. We had a dehumidifier break down last month, and the humidity spiked to 60% for a whole weekend. I was beside myself. I had to call the emergency HVAC guy, and of course, it was a Sunday, so they charged time and a half. The budget committee had an absolute fit about the overtime charge. They act like I broke the machine on purpose just to spend their money. 

But anyway, what was I... oh, right, work. Yes, it's definitely interfering. I actually had to hand off parts of a major grant presentation last month because I just... I froze. My mind went completely blank, and I couldn't stop thinking about all the things that could go wrong if we didn't get the funding. My assistant had to step in and finish the slides. It was so embarrassing. It’s just not like me at all, and now I’m constantly worrying about whether I can even keep leading my team well. They rely on me, you know? And if I'm freezing up over a presentation, how am I supposed to manage the whole department?
Do you feel like your worrying is causing you a lot of distress or discomfort?

Yes, absolutely. It's... it's exhausting. I just feel this constant, heavy knot in my stomach all the time, and my shoulders are always tight. I actually tried getting a massage for it last week, which I never do, but I was just so desperate for some relief. 

The massage therapist was lovely, but she used this lavender oil that was incredibly strong. It smelled exactly like the sachets my grandmother used to keep in her linen closet. She had this beautiful old cedar chest where she stored all the quilts she made by hand. The craftsmanship was unbelievable—tiny, perfect stitches. We actually have a small textile exhibit coming up at the library, focusing on local quilting traditions from the 19th century. Getting the display cases for that has been a nightmare, by the way. The glass has to be UV-filtering, and the vendor sent the wrong specifications twice. I spent three hours on the phone with their customer service department, and the representative kept putting me on hold to play this awful, tinny elevator music. 

But, um... yes, the distress. It's really awful. It just feels like I'm constantly on edge, waiting for the other shoe to drop, and I can't ever just relax and feel okay.
Do you ever feel an overwhelming urge to check or recheck things, like locks or appliances?

Well, no, not really. I don't have that urge to keep checking things over and over like that. I mean, I lock the door when I leave, and that's usually it. 

Though, speaking of locks, the security system at the library has been acting up again. It's this older system, installed maybe fifteen years ago, and the keypads are just completely worn out. The numbers on the buttons are rubbed off, so you have to just memorize the pattern. The new security guard—he's a very nice young man, just out of college, I think—he keeps accidentally triggering the silent alarm because he forgets the code. The police have shown up twice this month already. It's terribly embarrassing. The chief of police actually called me directly last time, and he was not pleased. He said if it happens again, they're going to start charging us a nuisance fee. 

And honestly, where are we supposed to find the money for a nuisance fee? The city just cut our funding by another five percent. They act like libraries are just obsolete, like everyone just gets everything on their phones now. But they don't see the people who come in every day to use the computers to apply for jobs, or the kids who need a safe place to go after school. It just breaks my heart how little they value what we do. 

But, um, anyway... no, I don't really have a problem with checking locks or appliances or anything like that. Just the normal amount, I suppose.
Is there one particular area in your life where your worries seem to be most concentrated?

Well, no, it's not just one area anymore. That's part of why I'm here. Over this past year, my worrying has just... spread. It used to be mostly about my mother's safety, which makes sense because she lives alone and she's getting older. 

But speaking of older houses, her house has these beautiful original hardwood floors, but they are so drafty in the winter. I’ve been trying to get a contractor out there to look at the subflooring, but it’s nearly impossible to get anyone to return a call these days. I finally got this one guy on the phone, and he started quoting me these outrageous prices just for an estimate. It reminded me of when we had to get the roof patched at the library after that terrible storm last spring. The wind just ripped the shingles right off the east wing. We had a bucket brigade going in the reference section for two days because the water was dripping right above the encyclopedia collection. Those encyclopedias are practically antiques themselves, you know. 

But anyway, what I mean is... the worry isn't just about my mother now. It's about everything. It's my finances, staff decisions at the library, deadlines for grants, the house... I even worry constantly about whether I’m being a good daughter. It feels like even the smallest things can start to feel like they’re just about to completely unravel.
Have you been avoiding any activities or situations because of your worries?

Um, avoiding things? No, I don't really think so. I mean, I still do everything I need to do, I just... I worry the whole time I'm doing them, I guess. 

Like, I still go to my Thursday evening book club. We meet at this little café downtown. Actually, right now we're reading this fascinating biography of Eleanor Roosevelt. Did you know she used to write a daily newspaper column? It was called 'My Day'. I was looking into it for a display we're putting together for Women's History Month, and I found out she wrote it six days a week for almost thirty years. That kind of dedication is just staggering. I can barely get my staff to submit their timesheets once a week! Brenda—she's one of the circulation assistants—she always forgets, and then she tries to backdate them in the system, which completely messes up the payroll software. The IT guy, David, gets so frustrated when he has to fix it. He has this nervous habit of clicking his pen repeatedly when he's annoyed, and it drives me absolutely up the wall. Click, click, click, the whole time he's resetting the database. 

But... I'm sorry, what was the question? Oh, avoiding situations. Right. No, I still go to work and run my errands and everything. I don't hide away. I just carry all this dread around with me wherever I go.
Has your worrying affected your relationships with friends or family members?

Affected my relationships? I... I don't really think so. I haven't noticed any big problems, anyway. I mean, my sister and I still talk every Sunday evening, like clockwork. 

She lives out in Portland now, and she's always telling me about her garden. She grows these absolutely incredible heirloom tomatoes. Cherokee Purples, I think they're called? They are so finicky, though. If they get too much water, the skins just split right open. Last year she had this terrible problem with aphids, and she tried using ladybugs to get rid of them. She actually ordered a whole box of live ladybugs through the mail! Can you imagine? The mail carrier must have been so confused delivering a buzzing cardboard box. 

Our mail carrier at the library, Tom, he's always complaining about the strange things people get shipped nowadays. Just last week, someone had a box of live crickets delivered for their pet lizard, and the box got crushed in transit. There were crickets loose in the staff breakroom for three days! We had to put out little sticky traps behind the microwave and the refrigerator. Brenda nearly fainted when one jumped onto her coffee mug while she was pouring her hazelnut creamer. 

But, um... wait, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Friends and family? Right. No, I think things are mostly fine with everyone. I haven't really noticed my worrying getting in the way of that.
Are you finding it harder to concentrate or make decisions at work due to your worrying?

Concentrate at work? Yes. Oh, absolutely. It's getting so frustrating. Like, during cataloging reviews or staff meetings, I’ll be looking right at the screen or the agenda, and suddenly I realize I haven’t absorbed a single word. My mind has just completely wandered off into some problem I think I should have prevented, or some disaster I need to fix. 

It's just like what happened with the Dewey Decimal update last month. We were trying to integrate the new classifications for computer science, and it is just a nightmare. The 004s and 005s are so crowded now. And don't even get me started on the shift they did with the 300s a few years back. The social sciences section is still a mess because we never had the budget to hire a temp to help with the relabeling. I actually found a whole stack of sociology journals from 1998 wedged behind a radiator in the basement archives when we were looking for space. The radiator was leaking, of course, because the maintenance guy, Phil, used the wrong sealant on the valve. Phil means well, but he's always trying to cut corners. He told me he learned plumbing from watching YouTube videos, which is just terrifying when you think about the fact that he's responsible for a building full of irreplaceable paper. 

But... wait, concentration. Right. Yeah, it's definitely harder. I just can't seem to keep my focus on what's right in front of me anymore.
Are there any situations or activities that you used to enjoy but now avoid because of your worrying?

Avoid things I used to enjoy? Um, no, I don't think I've stopped doing anything like that. I still keep up with my hobbies and everything. 

Like, I still do my watercolor painting on Sunday afternoons. I've been working on this series of botanical prints, mostly local wildflowers. Actually, getting the right shade of yellow for goldenrod is surprisingly difficult. You'd think yellow is just yellow, but if you don't mix in a tiny bit of purple, it looks completely flat and unnatural. I buy my paints from this little independent art supply shop over on 4th Street. The owner, Margaret, she just adopted this rescue parrot that she keeps in the shop now. It's an African Grey, and it mimics the sound of the barcode scanner perfectly. It is so confusing when you're trying to check out. Last time I was there, the poor cashier—this teenager who looked like he'd rather be anywhere else—scanned my cadmium red paint three times because the bird kept making the beep noise and he thought the register wasn't catching it. He had to call Margaret over to void the transaction, and it took twenty minutes because she couldn't remember her manager override password. She keeps it written on a sticky note under the keyboard, but the parrot actually chewed the corner off the note, so the last two numbers were completely gone...

Wait, I'm sorry, I completely lost my train of thought. What did you ask me? Oh, avoiding activities. Right. No, I haven't really given up anything I enjoy. I still do it all, I just... I might be worrying the whole time I'm painting, but I still do it.
Are there any situations that you're not avoiding, but perhaps wish you could avoid, because of your worrying?

Wish I could avoid? Um... I don't really know. I don't think there's anything specific I wish I could just stop doing completely. I mean, I have to go to work, obviously, and I have to run errands. 

Like grocery shopping. I still go to the grocery store every Thursday evening. I try to go around 7:00 because that's when they restock the produce, but lately, they've been so inconsistent. Last week, I went in to get some of those little cocktail cucumbers, and the entire section was just empty. The produce manager, Dave—he’s this guy who always wears these really loud Hawaiian shirts, even in the dead of winter—he said their delivery truck broke down on the interstate. Apparently, the radiator just blew right out. Which reminds me, my own car has been making this awful rattling noise whenever I go over 40 miles an hour. I took it to the mechanic, and he said it was the heat shield, but I'm just not sure I trust him. He had this waiting room that smelled strongly of stale popcorn and pine Sol, and the magazines were all from 2018. Who keeps a five-year-old copy of Field & Stream in a waiting room? I started reading this article about fly fishing in Montana, and it was actually fascinating. They use these tiny little hand-tied flies that look exactly like real insects. People spend hours just tying feathers and thread onto hooks with tweezers and a magnifying glass...

But, um, what were we talking about? Oh, right, wishing I could avoid things. No, I don't think there's anything I'm forcing myself through that I wish I could just drop. I just sort of power through the day, you know?
Have you noticed your worrying affecting your relationships with friends or family in any significant way?

Affecting my relationships? Um, no, I wouldn't say that. My friends and family are pretty understanding, and we still see each other just as much. I don't think my worrying has put a wedge between us or anything. 

Like, I just saw my sister, Elaine, this past weekend. We went to this new brunch place downtown. They took over the old Woolworth's building, which is actually kind of a tragedy because that building had original Art Deco crown molding that they just completely painted over with this awful, trendy matte gray. Everyone is obsessed with gray these days. Elaine actually just painted her entire living room this color called "Agreeable Gray." It took her three trips to the hardware store because the guy at the paint counter kept mixing the base wrong. He was this young kid who was completely distracted by his phone, watching some video with the volume all the way up. I swear, nobody pays attention to detail anymore. Elaine was so mad she almost asked for the manager, but you know, she hates confrontation. Which is always so funny to me, because when we were kids, she was the one who would always argue with our mother about curfew. Mom had this strict 10 PM rule, even on weekends, which was just ridiculous when we were in high school. We lived in this tiny cul-de-sac where absolutely nothing ever happened anyway. I think the biggest neighborhood scandal was when Mr. Henderson's golden retriever dug up Mrs. Gable's prize-winning petunias. She was so proud of those petunias, she had them imported from some special nursery in Oregon...

Oh, dear, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I am so sorry, my mind just completely drifted off. What was the question? Oh, my relationships. Right. No, I haven't noticed any big issues with my family or my friends. Everything is pretty much fine on that front.
Are you finding it harder to fulfill your responsibilities at work or in your personal life because of your worrying?

Responsibilities? Oh, well... yes, actually. I hate to admit it, but work has been getting harder. I'm a librarian, and I've been missing these small but really important details lately. Like miscoding new acquisitions, which messes up the entire cataloging system. And last week, I had to do this presentation for a community literacy grant, and I just... froze. I completely blanked and had to hand off my section to my assistant director. 

Which was so embarrassing because he's only been with us for three months. He came from this tiny rural library system up in Vermont. He was telling me about it the other day—they didn't even have an automated checkout system until 2019. They were still using the old stamp cards! Remember those? With the little date due cards tucked into the back pocket of the book? I always loved the sound that stamp made. *Ka-chunk, ka-chunk.* It was so satisfying. My childhood librarian, Mrs. Higgins, she had this massive ink pad that always smelled faintly of licorice. I don't know why, maybe she kept candy in her desk. She was the one who actually got me into archiving. She showed me how to use the microfiche machine when I was ten. Microfiche is completely obsolete now, of course, everything is digitized. We just sent our last three machines to a recycling center that specializes in e-waste. The guy who came to pick them up drove this massive box truck that barely fit in our loading dock. He had to back up and pull forward like six times, and he ended up scraping the yellow paint right off one of the safety bollards. Our facilities manager was absolutely furious. He just repainted those bollards in May. He used this special reflective industrial paint that costs like eighty dollars a gallon...

Oh, goodness, I'm doing it again. I'm so sorry. I just... my mind just races. What were we talking about? Work responsibilities. Right. Yes, I froze during the grant presentation, and it's just not like me at all. It's really making me worry about whether I can even keep leading my team properly if I can't even get through a basic presentation without panicking.
Do you feel like your worrying is making it difficult for you to enjoy time with friends or family?

Enjoy time with them? Um, no, I don't think so. When I'm actually with them, I think I enjoy it just fine. I mean, we still laugh and have a good time. Like when I saw Elaine, we had a really nice brunch, despite the whole crown molding tragedy. 

Oh, and we actually ordered these incredible lemon ricotta pancakes. They came with this blueberry compote that was just out of this world. The waitress said they source all their berries from this local farm out in the valley. I tried growing blueberries once, back when Jim and I first bought the house. We put in these three bushes along the back fence, but the soil there is just too alkaline, I think. Plus, the neighborhood squirrels are absolutely ruthless. They would wait until the berries were perfectly ripe, and then just strip the bushes bare in a single morning. One time, I actually caught this one really fat squirrel sitting on the fence post, just holding a blueberry in its little paws and staring right at me while he ate it. It was like he was mocking me! I ended up buying this special netting to put over the bushes, but it was such a hassle to take off every time I wanted to water them. And then a bird got tangled in it—a poor little sparrow. I had to go out there with scissors and carefully cut it loose. It was terrified, its little heart was beating so fast. I felt so guilty I just took all the netting down and let the squirrels have the rest. Which is probably for the best, because Jim ended up building a tool shed right over that spot anyway. He bought one of those pre-fab kits from the home improvement store, but the instructions were completely incomprehensible. It took him three weekends just to get the foundation level...

Wait, what was the question? Oh, my goodness, I am so sorry. You asked if I was enjoying my time with family. Yes, yes, I still enjoy seeing them. The worrying doesn't really stop me from having a good time once I'm actually there.
Do you feel like you have to think certain thoughts or perform certain actions in a specific, repetitive way to try and relieve your anxiety?

Repetitive actions? Like, um, rituals or something? No, I don't think I do anything like that. I just worry. I don't have to, like, wash my hands a certain number of times or check the locks over and over. 

Though speaking of locks, we actually just had to replace the deadbolt on our front door. The old one was getting so sticky, you had to jiggle the key just right, and pull the handle toward you at the exact same time, or it wouldn't turn. Jim kept saying he was going to spray some WD-40 in it, but he never got around to it. He's always starting these little projects around the house and then just... leaving them halfway done. Like the time he decided to regrout the guest bathroom. He scraped all the old grout out, which made a huge mess—there was fine white dust everywhere, it even got into the hallway carpet. And then he realized he bought the wrong color grout. He bought "Antique White" instead of "Bright White," and let me tell you, there is a very noticeable difference. Antique White looks almost yellow, like someone smoked in the bathroom for twenty years. So he had to go back to the hardware store, but they were completely sold out of Bright White, and they said it would take two weeks to order it in. So we just had this unusable, dusty bathroom for half a month. We had my mother-in-law coming to visit, too, and she is incredibly particular about cleanliness. She used to run a bed and breakfast up in Maine, right on the coast. It was this gorgeous Victorian house with a wrap-around porch, but the upkeep was just astronomical. The sea salt in the air practically eats through exterior paint. She had to have the whole place scraped and repainted every three years, and she always hired this one specific crew...

Oh, I'm so sorry. I'm rambling again, aren't I? I don't know why I do this. What did you ask me? Oh, right, repetitive thoughts or actions. No, I don't have anything like that. Just the worrying.
Do you feel like your worrying is significantly interfering with your ability to function at work or in social situations?

Yes, absolutely. Like I was saying just a few minutes ago—before I went on that whole tangent about the loading dock, sorry—it really is affecting my work. Missing those small, important details with the cataloging is just so unlike me. And freezing up during that grant presentation... it really shook me. Having to hand my part over to my assistant director because I couldn't speak was awful. 

Which, by the way, that grant is so crucial for our summer reading program. We're doing an "Oceans of Possibility" theme this year, and I had already ordered all these inflatable sea creatures to hang from the ceiling in the children's section. Do you know how hard it is to find a reasonably priced inflatable squid? I had to scour the internet for days, and when it finally arrived, it smelled so strongly of cheap vinyl. I tried airing it out in the staff breakroom, but then the whole room smelled like a pool toy factory, and Brenda—she's our circulation clerk—she gets terrible migraines from strong smells. She actually had to go home early on Tuesday because of it. She takes this special medication that makes her really drowsy, so she can't even drive when she takes it, her husband has to come pick her up. He drives this immaculate vintage Mustang, it's really quite beautiful, cherry red with these white racing stripes down the middle. He said he restored the engine completely by himself, which I always find so impressive because I don't know the first thing about cars. I can barely remember to get my oil changed...

Oh, dear. I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? I am so sorry. But yes, to answer your question, the worrying is definitely interfering with my functioning. Freezing up like that at the presentation... it just really makes me question if I can even keep leading my team well when I'm like this.
Do you feel like your worrying is causing you significant distress or interfering with your ability to function in your daily life or at work?

I feel like we might have just touched on this a second ago, but yes, it really is causing me a lot of distress. Like I was saying, it’s the work stuff that bothers me the most. I've started missing these small but really important details at the library, which is just so completely unlike me. 

Just last week, I completely messed up the spine labels on a whole cart of new arrivals. I put this beautiful new biography of Eleanor Roosevelt in the completely wrong section. And Mrs. Higgins, one of our regulars, actually had to point it out to me. She reads a lot of history because her grandfather was in World War II. He was stationed in England, and she actually brought in this old black-and-white photograph of him once, standing next to a military jeep. It’s amazing how well preserved those old photos can be if you keep them out of the sunlight. We actually have a whole local history archive in the basement of the library, and the climate control down there is just a nightmare to maintain. The HVAC system is from the eighties, and it makes this horrible clanking sound every time it kicks on. We've had the repair guy, Dave, out three times this month, and he always tracks mud onto the carpet near the reference desk. I bought one of those heavy-duty rubber mats to put down, but people keep tripping over the corner because it won't lay flat... 

Oh, goodness, I am so sorry, I'm doing it again. I just can't seem to keep my train of thought on track today. But yes, to go back to what you asked—and what I was saying before about the presentation—the distress is very real. Having to hand off parts of that grant presentation to my assistant director after I completely froze up... it honestly just terrifies me. It makes me worry so much about whether I can even keep leading my team well when I'm functioning like this.
Are you finding it harder to interact with your colleagues or supervise your team at work due to your worrying?

I feel like a bit of a broken record today, but yes, it really is. Like I keep mentioning with that grant presentation—having to hand off parts of it to my assistant director after I completely froze up... it honestly just makes me worry so much about whether I can keep leading my team well. They rely on me, you know? And missing those small but important details around the library lately is just not like me at all, and I know the staff notices. 

I supervise about twelve people total, including our part-time student pages. We have this one page, Kevin, who is a sweet kid—he's studying graphic design over at the community college—but he always listens to his headphones while he's shelving books. He listens to these true crime podcasts. They are incredibly popular right now, actually. We had to set up a whole separate endcap display just for true crime paperbacks because people kept coming in and asking for them. I ordered this really nice, tiered acrylic display stand for it, but when it arrived, the shipping box looked like it had been run over by a delivery truck. The acrylic was completely cracked right down the middle. I had to spend forty-five minutes on hold with the distributor's customer service line just to get a replacement authorized. And their hold music was this awful, synthesized pan flute that just loops the exact same eight bars over and over until you feel like you're going completely mad...

Oh, dear, I am so sorry. I'm rambling again, aren't I? My brain just keeps taking these detours today. But yes, interacting with the staff and supervising them is definitely getting harder. When I'm freezing up and missing things like I have been, it just really makes me doubt my ability to keep leading them properly.

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I came in because once a worry starts—about my mother getting up at night, a grant report, or whether I missed something at work—I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself.

patient.answer:

patient.answer:
Yes, absolutely. Like I was saying just a few minutes ago—before I went on that whole tangent about the loading dock, sorry—it really is affecting my work. Missing those small, important details with the cataloging is just so unlike me. And freezing up during that grant presentation... it really shook me. Having to hand my part over to my assistant director because I couldn't speak was awful. 

Which, by the way, that grant is so crucial for our summer reading program. We're doing an "Oceans of Possibility" theme this year, and I had already ordered all these inflatable sea creatures to hang from the ceiling in the children's section. Do you know how hard it is to find a reasonably priced inflatable squid? I had to scour the internet for days, and when it finally arrived, it smelled so strongly of cheap vinyl. I tried airing it out in the staff breakroom, but then the whole room smelled like a pool toy factory, and Brenda—she's our circulation clerk—she gets terrible migraines from strong smells. She actually had to go home early on Tuesday because of it. She takes this special medication that makes her really drowsy, so she can't even drive when she takes it, her husband has to come pick her up. He drives this immaculate vintage Mustang, it's really quite beautiful, cherry red with these white racing stripes down the middle. He said he restored the engine completely by himself, which I always find so impressive because I don't know the first thing about cars. I can barely remember to get my oil changed...

Oh, dear. I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? I am so sorry. But yes, to answer your question, the worrying is definitely interfering with my functioning. Freezing up like that at the presentation... it just really makes me question if I can even keep leading my team well when I'm like this.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Do you feel like your worrying is causing you significant distress or interfering with your ability to function in your daily life or at work?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve started missing small but important details at the library and had to hand off parts of a grant presentation after I froze, which is not like me and has made me worry about whether I can keep leading my team well.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the worrying causes significant distress or interferes with my ability to function at work or in daily life, which directly maps to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I feel like we might have just touched on this a second ago, but yes, it really is causing me a lot of distress. Like I was saying, it’s the work stuff that bothers me the most. I've started missing these small but really important details at the library, which is just so completely unlike me. 

Just last week, I completely messed up the spine labels on a whole cart of new arrivals. I put this beautiful new biography of Eleanor Roosevelt in the completely wrong section. And Mrs. Higgins, one of our regulars, actually had to point it out to me. She reads a lot of history because her grandfather was in World War II. He was stationed in England, and she actually brought in this old black-and-white photograph of him once, standing next to a military jeep. It’s amazing how well preserved those old photos can be if you keep them out of the sunlight. We actually have a whole local history archive in the basement of the library, and the climate control down there is just a nightmare to maintain. The HVAC system is from the eighties, and it makes this horrible clanking sound every time it kicks on. We've had the repair guy, Dave, out three times this month, and he always tracks mud onto the carpet near the reference desk. I bought one of those heavy-duty rubber mats to put down, but people keep tripping over the corner because it won't lay flat... 

Oh, goodness, I am so sorry, I'm doing it again. I just can't seem to keep my train of thought on track today. But yes, to go back to what you asked—and what I was saying before about the presentation—the distress is very real. Having to hand off parts of that grant presentation to my assistant director after I completely froze up... it honestly just terrifies me. It makes me worry so much about whether I can even keep leading my team well when I'm functioning like this.

doctor.question: Are you finding it harder to interact with your colleagues or supervise your team at work due to your worrying?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulties at work, specifically interacting with colleagues and supervising the team, which directly relates to my functional impairment and concerns about leading my team well.

patient.answer:
I feel like a bit of a broken record today, but yes, it really is. Like I keep mentioning with that grant presentation—having to hand off parts of it to my assistant director after I completely froze up... it honestly just makes me worry so much about whether I can keep leading my team well. They rely on me, you know? And missing those small but important details around the library lately is just not like me at all, and I know the staff notices. 

I supervise about twelve people total, including our part-time student pages. We have this one page, Kevin, who is a sweet kid—he's studying graphic design over at the community college—but he always listens to his headphones while he's shelving books. He listens to these true crime podcasts. They are incredibly popular right now, actually. We had to set up a whole separate endcap display just for true crime paperbacks because people kept coming in and asking for them. I ordered this really nice, tiered acrylic display stand for it, but when it arrived, the shipping box looked like it had been run over by a delivery truck. The acrylic was completely cracked right down the middle. I had to spend forty-five minutes on hold with the distributor's customer service line just to get a replacement authorized. And their hold music was this awful, synthesized pan flute that just loops the exact same eight bars over and over until you feel like you're going completely mad...

Oh, dear, I am so sorry. I'm rambling again, aren't I? My brain just keeps taking these detours today. But yes, interacting with the staff and supervising them is definitely getting harder. When I'm freezing up and missing things like I have been, it just really makes me doubt my ability to keep leading them properly.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of excessive and pervasive worry about everyday things, difficulty controlling the worry, and significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life are consistent with Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD). The patient does not exhibit symptoms of repetitive behaviors or mental acts aimed at preventing or reducing distress, which is more characteristic of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD).
